section_summary: This section consists of State Department records from 1940 and 1943 concerning Japanese cultural relations, propaganda, and education policies filed under decimal file 894.427. The primary document is an extensive 45-page research report prepared in January 1943 by the Division of Cultural Relations based on FCC shortwave broadcast monitoring, which provides a comprehensive survey of Japan's 1942 cultural offensive, educational and religious reorganization, Japanese language promotion, media control, exchanges of scholars and students, and bilateral cultural agreements across the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere. The section also includes the Department's March 1943 instruction transmitting this report to the American Embassy in Chungking, as well as a March 1940 Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing the status, numbers, and Japanese governmental exploitation of American citizens of Japanese ancestry residing in Japan.

subfiles.about: Diplomatic instruction transmitting a Division of Cultural Relations memorandum on Japan's 1942 cultural relations program to the American Embassy in Chungking.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to the American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Chungking, China, a copy of a strictly confidential memorandum prepared in the China Section of the Division of Cultural Relations entitled 'Japan's Program of Cultural Relations, 1942'. The transmittal serves to inform the Embassy of Japanese cultural strategies and wartime policy developments across East Asia.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 257 to the American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Chungking, Transmitting Memorandum on Japan's Program of Cultural Relations, 1942
subfiles.to: The American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Chungking, China

subfiles.about: A comprehensive State Department report surveying Japanese cultural propaganda, educational control, language instruction, and cultural diplomacy across occupied Asia during 1942 based on shortwave radio monitoring.
subfiles.from: Haldore Hanson and William H. Dennis, China Section, Division of Cultural Relations
subfiles.summary: Prepared by Haldore Hanson and William H. Dennis for Division Chief Charles A. Thomson, this comprehensive 45-page report examines Japan's wartime cultural program throughout the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere in 1942 based on shortwave broadcasts recorded by the FCC's Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service. It details the administrative and budgetary apparatus behind Japanese cultural warfare, including educational realignment, press and radio control, compulsory Japanese language teaching, religious manipulation, and the activities of newly created cultural societies. The report further reviews the exchange of students, teachers, writers, and scientists, exhibitions of art and aviation, technical agricultural aid, and bilateral treaties, providing the complete text of the October 1942 Japan-Thailand Cultural Agreement. The authors conclude that Japan's vigorous cultural program has significantly dismantled Western influence and will necessitate a robust, expert-led American cultural relations counter-effort during and after the war.
subfiles.title: Japan's Program of Cultural Relations, 1942
subfiles.to: Charles A. Thomson, Chief, Division of Cultural Relations

subfiles.about: A State Department memorandum analyzing a consular report from Yokohama regarding the demographics, social integration, and Japanese governmental exploitation of American citizens of Japanese descent living in Japan.
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: This memorandum by Cabot Coville reviews a voluntary report of January 29, 1940, submitted by Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama concerning American citizens of Japanese ancestry residing in Japan. It analyzes two distinct groups: an estimated 25,000 to 100,000 largely uneducated Nisei living primarily in the Kobe consular district who show little inclination to return to the United States, and approximately 1,500 American-educated citizens concentrated in Tokyo who arrived mainly after 1933. The memorandum observes that the Japanese government and organizations like the America-Japan Society have cultivated this latter group to employ their English skills in international propaganda, while simultaneously taking steps via radio and other media to discourage further migration of Japanese-Americans to Japan and attempting to convince them that American culture is inferior.
subfiles.title: American Citizens of Japanese Race Residing in Japan
